title: Setting on the Path of Deep Learning with fastai, lesson 1
text:
Like many who have come before , I’m starting on the path of deep learning with fastai and their brilliant freely available course and companion book. One of their first recommendations, other than learning how to learn, is to start a blog. Why? Because there’s no learning like reflection and teaching. Yes, it seems to run counter to the experience many of us had in school - focusing on rote memorization and regurgitation.1

The long and short of it: the best way to learn, is to do. 2 So here we go.

Started with the lesson 1 notebook on Kaggle, walked through the lesson, then copied it to build my own first classifier!
Now, let’s just state up front: it’s not very good. The intent was to build a classifier for various species of poisonous mushroom. The problem is, many of the them look alike; so much so that the model thought it had nearly 100% accuracy on exactly the wrong species. For example, when asks to classify a fool’s funnel, the model thought it was almost exactly like the death cap. They are two different species; clearly more training or tuning is required.
Initially, I used 3 different species, but it created more confusion for the model than desired. The current iteration uses only 2 species, and the model executed over 20 iterations or epochs. The results were far better this time around.

The training loss converges to just above 0, with the error_rate following suite. The valid_loss settles on 0.26, which indicates the model is a bit loss-y, so to speak.

The model maintains a 100% probability when identifying death cap mushrooms:



This is a: death cap.

Not so accurate when classifying fly agaric:




This is a: fly agaric.
Probability it's a fly agaric: 0.0031
The probability of accuracy is tiny, but still correct.

At this point, it’s unclear what steps to take to improve the result for fly agaric classification. It could be there aren’t enough distinctions between the samples in the data set, rendering them too similar for the model to tell the difference. As this is the beginning, refining and training models and analysing output can only get better.

Head on over to Kaggle to interact the fully-functional notebook.

Thanks for reading. Onward and upward.

title: CTF Forensics Write-Up: Trivial Flag Transfer Protocol
CTF Forensics Write-Up: Trivial Flag Transfer Protocol
text:
1. Challenge Overview & Objectives

Prompt Description: > “Figure out how they moved the flag. tftp.pcapng”
Core Questions Answered:

What are some other ways to hide data? Combining classical substitution ciphers (ROT-13) with image steganography (steghide) over an unencrypted transport protocol (TFTP).
Based on the title, what files are transferred? Six files transferred via Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP): instructions.txt, plan, program.deb, picture1.bmp, picture2.bmp, and picture3.bmp.
Where is the flag hidden? Embedded inside picture3.bmp using steghide and protected with a passphrase recovered from the network traffic.

3. Environment & Tooling

OS / Analysis VM: Kali Linux
Tools Used: Wireshark, CyberChef, binwalk, strings, exiftool, steghide, zsteg, dCode.fr, Aperi’Solve

title: CTF Forensics Write-Up: Trivial Flag Transfer Protocol
text:
4. Investigation Log & Confirmed Findings

Step 1: Initial Triage

Commands Run:
$ file tftp.pcapng
$ exiftool -a -u -g1 -ee3 -api RetrieveAll=3 tftp.pcapng
$ strings -n 8 tftp.pcapng | grep -i "academy"
Findings: Confirmed a valid pcapng network capture. No plaintext flag strings were present in the raw packet data.



Step 2: Network Traffic & TFTP Extraction (Wireshark)

TFTP Write Request (instructions.txt):

Observation: Packet 3 is a TFTP transfer from 10.10.10.11:34790 to 10.10.10.12:52355.
Extracted Data: Identified ROT-13 ciphertext and decoded it using dCode ROT-13:

TFTP DOESNT ENCRYPT OUR TRAFFIC SO WE MUST DISGUISE OUR FLAG TRANSFER. FIGURE OUT A WAY TO HIDE THE FLAG AND I WILL CHECK BACK FOR THE PLAN


TFTP Read Request (plan):

Observation: Packet 20 revealed a 59-byte TFTP data transfer from 10.10.10.12:41165 to 10.10.10.11:44157.
Extracted Data: Decoded the ROT-13 ciphertext to reveal the steganography passphrase ([REDACTED]):

I USED THE PROGRAM AND HID IT WITH - [REDACTED]. CHECK OUT THE PHOTOS


Bulk Object Extraction:

Action: Used File > Export Objects > TFTP in Wireshark to extract all transferred files (instructions.txt, plan, program.deb, picture1.bmp, picture2.bmp, and picture3.bmp) to a local working directory.




Step 3: Package & Steganography Analysis

Debian Package Inspection (program.deb):

Observation: Ran binwalk -Mek program.deb (or dpkg -I program.deb) to identify the software transferred over TFTP.
Finding: Confirmed the package was steghide, indicating the exact tool used to embed data into the BMP images.

Image Triage (picture1.bmp – picture3.bmp):

Observation: Standard metadata (exiftool) and strings checks returned no anomalies. Running zsteg -a flagged potential OpenPGP/binary data at the end of picture3.bmp, confirming hidden payload presence.

title: CTF Forensics Write-Up: Trivial Flag Transfer Protocol
text:
5. Solution & Flag Extraction

Step-by-Step Solve Path

Open tftp.pcapng in Wireshark and extract all TFTP objects via File > Export Objects > TFTP.
Decode the contents of instructions.txt and plan using ROT-13 to uncover the passphrase ([REDACTED]).
Inspect program.deb with binwalk to confirm steghide was used to hide the payload.
Extract the hidden flag file from picture3.bmp using steghide:
$ steghide extract -sf picture3.bmp -p [REDACTED]
Read the extracted flag.txt file to obtain the final flag.



Decoded Flag
academy{REDACTED}

Transferring the steghide Debian installer (program.deb) across the network to stage the steganography utility.

Using cleartext UDP-based TFTP to move the steganographically disguised flag out of the environment.

title: CTF Forensics Write-Up: Trivial Flag Transfer Protocol
text:
7. Key Takeaways & Lessons Learned

Protocol Awareness: TFTP transmits files in cleartext over UDP, making Wireshark’s Export Objects feature the fastest way to reconstruct transferred payloads.
Tool Correlation: Always inspect accompanying binaries or installers (program.deb) in a capture—they directly reveal the encoding or steganography tool used by the threat actor.
Read Clues Carefully: The passphrase was hidden in plain sight inside the decoded plan message rather than requiring brute-force cracking.
Steganography Tooling: While zsteg is great for detecting LSB anomalies and appended data in PNG/BMP files, steghide uses a pseudo-random bit-distribution algorithm that requires the matching tool and passphrase for extraction.
